Sanjay, good video and you raised some important points, but I don't fully agree with your analysis. 
 
First, Google and Amazon are not doing badly as businesses. Their revenue is growing, especially in cloud and AI. Yes, they are spending huge money on AI data centres, and that is something to watch carefully. But spending more cash doesn't automatically mean the business is losing money or that AI is failing. We need to give these investments some time to show results. 
 
Also, Amazon's negative $42 billion free cash flow is for 12 months, not just one quarter. That's quite a big difference. 
 
Regarding gold, it's not unusual for gold and stocks to fall together when there is panic in the market. Sometimes big investors need cash and sell whatever they can. It doesn't mean diversification has stopped working. 
 
One thing I found a bit strange was that you advised people to protect their wealth and be careful, but then promoted futures trading with 5x or even 100x leverage. Isn't that the opposite of being careful? An inexperienced investor can lose a lot of money very quickly doing this. 
 
I also think we shouldn't mix too much political speculation with investment decisions. Elections come and go, markets react, and then businesses carry on. 
 
For me, the real question is whether Google, Amazon and Microsoft will eventually make good returns from all this AI spending. That's what matters over the next 5–10 years. 
 
I believe long-term investors should focus on good companies, reasonable prices and strong balance sheets rather than getting worried about every market correction. 
 
I enjoyed the discussion, but I think the situation is not as bad as the video makes it sound. A little more balance would make your analysis even better.

Are Retail Investors Being Taught Technical Analysis to Help Them Make Money, or to Make Them Easier Targets?

Think about it.

Retail investors are encouraged to learn technical analysis, identify support and resistance levels, draw trendlines, follow indicators, and predict market movements.

But here's the bigger picture: large institutional investors, operators, and market participants often have significantly more capital, better technology, faster execution, and access to deeper market data.

They understand where retail traders are likely to place their stop-losses, where breakout buyers enter, and where panic selling begins.

Sometimes, what looks like a perfect breakout turns into a trap. What appears to be a strong support level gets broken, triggering thousands of stop-losses before the price reverses.

The real game isn't always about predicting the market. It's about understanding how other market participants react.

Technical analysis is not useless, but blindly following charts, indicators, and popular trading strategies can make retail investors predictable.

Don't just learn how to read charts. Learn how the market works, how liquidity moves, and how institutional players operate.

Remember: If you cannot identify the game, you might unknowingly become part of someone else's strategy.
